BMS 500: This hands-on course teaches students a variety of fundamental skills required to successfully conduct independent biomedical research.
BMS 501: Teaches biochemical and signal transduction concepts while exploring the control of bioenergetic processes.
BMS 502: This course will cover the cellular basis of physiological processes from a systemic perspective.
BMS 503: This course will provide fundamental and applied knowledge in the broadly defined area of molecular genetics.
BMS 504: Introduction to scientific analysis, writing, and oral presentation using primary literature sources.
BMS 505: Advanced topics in scientific analysis, writing, and oral presentation using primary literature sources.
BMS 506A: Cellular, molecular, genetic, and biochemical basis of organ function pathology.
BMS 506B: Cellular, molecular, genetic, and biochemical basis of organ function pathology.
BMS 507: The focus of this course is on the architecture of biological macromolecules that constitute all living cells.
BMS 508: This course will provide fundamental and applied knowledge in the broadly defined area of metabolism.
BMS 512: Biology is becoming increasingly computational as new technologies are producing massive amounts of data.
BMS 520: This course explores whole organ physiology emphasizing skeletal muscle and exercise physiology, cardiovascular, renal and urinary, respiratory, gastrointestinal, and endocrine.
BMS 550: Tumorigenesis is a multistep process driven by genetic and molecular changes that occur over time.
BMS 551: Genomic instability is a major hallmark of carcinogenesis.
BMS 552: Cancer is a disease of dysregulation of cellular growth machinery leading to loss of growth suppressive mechanisms, increased growth promoting signaling, and other key hallmarks supporting the clonal expansion of malignant cells.
BMS 553: Students will be exposed to a range of topics in cancer biology from the primary literature to expand their knowledge of current state-of-the art research in cancer biology, and to enhance their critical thinking skills and ability to critique the primary literature.
BMS 554: This course gives students an overview of the fundamental processes leading to cancer development but with a focus on using drugs, immunological approaches, or interventions to combat these processes.
BMS 562: Investigation of diseases associated with immune system dysfunction and the manipulation of this system to prevent and treat disease.
BMS 564: The objective of the Concepts in Virology course is to describe the lifecycle of representative RNA and DNA viruses and the relationship between the virus and the host at the molecular level.
BMS 566: This course will provide an understanding of the role of viruses in the development of cancer in humans and the molecular mechanisms involved.
BMS 567: This course addresses methodologies used to study viral pathogenesis and recent advances in the field.
BMS 568: Current Topics in Translational Cancer Research is designed to prepare students to be the next generation of translational cancer researchers.
BMS 571: This course allows graduate students at Hershey and University Park to gain experience in the clinical arena.
BMS 581: This course teaches students the scientific process used to understand the molecular bases of diseases and the development of novel therapies.
BMS 590: Continuing seminars that consist of a series of individual lectures by faculty, students, or outside speakers.
BMS 591: Education in research ethics for biomedical scientists.
BMS 595: Supervised off-campus, nongroup instruction, including field experiences, practicums, or internships.
BMS 596: Creative projects, including nonthesis research, that are supervised on an individual basis and which fall outside the scope of formal courses.
BMS 597: Formal courses given on a topical or special interest subject which may be offered infrequently; several different topics may be taught in one year or semester.
BMS 597I: Formal courses given on a topical or special interest subject which may be offered infrequently; several different topics may be taught in one year or semester.
BMS 601: BMS 601 is available to full-time Ph.D.-degree candidates who have passed the comprehensive examination and met the two-semester residence requirement.
BMS 610: Off-campus laboratory work on thesis project.
BMS 801: This course will give students experience with the preparation of and submission process for grant proposals.
BMS 802: Translational Research in Medicine (BMS 802) is a mentorship course that provides post-comprehensive MD/PhD graduate students with the opportunity to work one-on-one with a clinician scientist mentor that will allow students to build upon and hone their clinical skills (history taking, physical exams).
